Furthermore, at the time of that Buddha, the assembly consisted exclusively of a single class of beings—only bodhisattvas. This gathering of seventy-six billion bodhisattvas was entirely non-retrogressive, having attained all the dhāraṇīs and emerged with eloquence.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin had a wheel-turning king named Puṇyavipula-viśuddha, who ruled over a thousand worlds; his treasuries and precious jewels were beyond measure."

Within the inner palace of his pure karmic retribution, there were eighty-four thousand ladies and court maids, all of whom were the most excellent celestial maidens (*yǔnǚ*) among the people of the land; the king had a thousand sons, all of whom were powerful warriors whose majesty was beyond description.

That king made offerings to the Great Sage Vīra for thirty-six billion years, providing all things that bring peace and security; meanwhile, the bodhisattvas offered him clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal treatments for illness and debility.
Śāriputra asked,
“Indeed, Great Sage!
How long was the lifespan of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"His lifespan was ten intermediate kalpas.

King Pure Merit made offerings to the Tathāgata Vipaśyin that were beyond measure. With his inner palace, sons, retinue, and kinsmen numbering ninety-two koṭis, he went to the Buddha Vipaśyin surrounded by attendants. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he offered a necklace of moon-bright pearls worth hundreds of thousands to the World-Honored One, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha Vipaśyin:"
"O Great Sage! Among all the offerings and requisites I possess, is there any offering that surpasses these which I present to the Tathāgata?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
The Tathāgata Vipaśyin replied to King Puṇyavanta-viśuddha: "Great King!
You should know that there is a distinct form of offering which is most honored, supreme, and peerless."

That which the King has not yet provided surpasses, by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, and even a myriad-billionfold, the articles of offering and worship previously bestowed by the King.
He asked again:
"What did the Tathāgata Vipaśyin perceive in the thoughts of that great king?
Then he spoke in verse:
“If one were to take billions of Buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas fill them with precious jewels to offer to the Tathāgatas, and were to combine all that merit;”
Those who do not pity sentient beings but instead give rise to the aspiration for the Way,
serve billions of buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
they honor them for countless billions of kalpas, likewise as numerous as the sands of the great rivers.
The Buddha’s path of compassionate mind is supreme; his seven steps were transcendent and extraordinary.
This is the offering to all Buddhas, the most honored, noble, and unsurpassed.
This giving is preeminent, as it enjoins immeasurable, supreme patience.
This diligence is firm and strong; concentration, mind, and wisdom are unshakable.
Those who give rise to the aspiration for the Way set their will and vows upon the Teacher;
this merit is most limitless, and that which has been accumulated can never be exhausted.
His fame spreads far and wide; his retinue is majestic and sublime;
his wealth, treasures, and power are magnificent; his heart’s every wish is as if obtained by fortune.
He becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King, with a majesty and power like that of Śakra or Brahmā.
If one’s disposition is joyful and glad, severing the mind from all [obstacles] through supernormal wisdom;
extinguishing all evil destinies, one will be entirely free from the fear of the eight difficulties;
increasing and benefiting the pure path, one shall always abide upon the way of gods and humans.
If a person establishes their resolve upon the stainless, unsurpassed path,
their faculties will always be clear and penetrating; with noble intelligence free from obstruction,
they shall behold all Buddhas, serve them, and hear the sūtras.
Diligently seeking the wisdom of the sages, they always know the mind that propagates the Way.
Their minds are free from hesitation and entanglement; they leave behind flattery and remain ever upright.
Out of compassion to rescue all sentient beings, their aspirations are set upon the resolve for the Path.
Not delighting in the pleasures of the senses, they aspire to the joy of the Dharma;
unattached to anything in all the world, their conduct is like a lotus in the water.
Never weary of merit and wisdom, they resolve to seek the *pāramitās*.
When one resolves for the Path in this way, who would not establish the Great Way?
Thus, with a great lamp and chain, they illuminate and rescue all the multitudes;
they become the most honored and supreme teacher, the great guide for all sentient beings!
He dwells as the most supreme in the world, dispensing medicine to eliminate all ailments;
he establishes the resolve for the Way, which is immeasurable, infinite, and inexhaustible.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

When King Pure Merit Reward heard the Tathāgata Vipaśyin speak on generating the aspiration for the Way, he marveled at the immeasurable nature of its merit; filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, he then gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the king’s inner court, the crown prince, the officials, the various ministers, and all the subordinate kings with their retinues followed in attendance and spoke these verses:
“Now we have established the most honored resolve for the Way;
we give rise to a heart of compassion, pitying and grieving for all sentient beings.”
If you wish to attain that which I hold in the highest esteem,
then arouse the aspiration for enlightenment and make it firm.
The original limit of birth and death cannot be known;
To sit and engage in unwholesome deeds leads to falling into suffering and affliction.
Diligently apply yourself with vigor, set your mind upon the Buddha-way,
and for the sake of sentient beings, practice compassion— how excellent!
Thus one can increase and benefit eloquence and wisdom;
fully providing such offerings, the noble and realized ones are like this.
The Buddha Vipaśyin attained that which is immeasurable.
With a mind of universal wisdom, his practice is such as this:
desiring to attain the peace and security of the heavenly realms, the state of Śakra, Brahmā,
or a Wheel-Turning Sage King— the peace of the conditioned and the bliss of the unconditioned.
One should then respectfully cultivate the intention for this Way.
Contemplating the gathering of dhyāna-concentration is immeasurable;
crossing over to the other shore, the Way is likewise so.
The sagely wisdom of penetration reaches everywhere;
such is the conduct of all those with omniscience.
The power of the Buddhas of the ten directions is inconceivable.
The four fearlessnesses are possessed by the Tathāgata.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is vast and boundless;
it is attained from a pure mind.
Even if one wishes to shake a thousand million lands,
their sounds are universally proclaimed so that all may hear and know.
Cultivating pure conduct, one expands it vast and stainless.
Those who are wise and discerning should give rise to the aspiration for the Way;
they will be honored and revered by those of the Ten Powers,
and all Tathāgatas will praise them with admiration!
For the sake of all sentient beings, he is a friend who needs no invitation;
those who possess wisdom and intelligence should give rise to the aspiration for the Way.
Even if the Buddha-way were to manifest without wisdom and compassion, [it would still be so].
To speak of its merits for countless billions of kalpas—
the merit and blessings inherent in the Buddha’s aspiration for the Way—
cannot be exhausted; how much less could one wish to limit them!

“At that time, as soon as King Pure Merit had spoken this verse, a multitude of ninety-two *koṭis* of people, along with the king’s harem and his thousand sons, conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). The trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and fourteen billion devas raised voices of exhortation and assistance, giving rise to the mind of the Great Way.”

Thereafter, that Wheel-Turning Sage King further reverently served the Honored One, the Tathāgata Vīra, for ten billion years. He bestowed all manner of offerings and peace, purely cultivating the holy life and the pure precepts. Constantly listening to the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, he went together with his retinue to receive the teachings of the Dharma. He then established his eldest son as the sovereign of the kingdom and, out of faith in the household life, shaved off his beard and hair, leaving home to practice the Way as a śramaṇa.
Having become a śramaṇa,
one immediately studies these four inexhaustible phrases, praising and extolling them in succession, seeking to attain them.
What are the four?
The chapters on utmost sincerity, the chapters on the Dharma-piṭaka, the chapters on sublime meaning, and the chapters on the disciplinary rules.

Having mastered these for billions of years through the application of skillful means, after that king left the household life to study them, he entered samādhi and correctly received the teachings within a thousand worlds to deliver sentient beings; they all became śramaṇas under the Tathāgata Vipaśyin.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If you wish to know who that Wheel-Turning Sage King with pure karmic retribution was at that time, could it be anyone else?
Do not harbor such a thought; she was none other than this Precious Woman!"
"This precious woman first resolved her mind upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the World-Honored One,
"By what karmic obstruction did she receive a female body?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not receive a female body because of the veil of offenses. Why is this? Because—”
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses wisdom, supernormal powers, skillful means, and noble clarity, he manifests in the form of a woman to transform and enlighten the masses.
What do you think, Śāriputra?
Is this precious woman truly a woman? Do not conceive such a view;
for she has manifested through the transformative power of the Sage’s supernormal faculties and is in fact a true Bodhisattva. You should rather conceive this view:
she possesses neither the dharma of a man nor the dharma of a woman, but is fully endowed with the essentials of all dharmas, coming from nowhere and going nowhere.
This Jewel Woman, while residing in Jambudvīpa, instructed and transformed ninety-two thousand young women, causing them all to resolve upon the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the Jewel Woman said to Śāriputra,
"Venerable sir, can you manifest in the body of a woman and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings?
Śāriputra replied:
"Now that I have this body of a man, which I do not delight in, how much less would I ever again accept the form of a woman?
The Jewel Woman asked,
"Do you feel loathing and revulsion for your own body?"
He then replied to the woman, saying,
"I am indeed weary and disgusted by it.
The Jewel Woman replied:
“Therefore, the Bodhisattva transcends all classes of sentient beings and has no equal.
Śāriputra asked: “For what reason?”
The girl replied, “Yes,
Śāriputra! That which would cause revulsion to those of the śrāvaka family, the bodhisattvas do not regard as a hardship.”
“What does the household of the śrāvaka find loathsome?
“The five aggregates (skandhas), the four great elements (mahābhūtas), and the matter of the six sense bases (āyatanas) are what the śrāvaka finds distressing;
the bodhisattva, however, maintains these five aggregates, four great elements, and six sense bases without regarding them as distressing.”
The śrāvakas feel loathing and revulsion toward their births, their worldly wanderings, and their grasping at a self;
the bodhisattvas, however, accept these bodies without any distress or aversion.
All the assemblies of śrāvakas detest the experience of birth and death.
The Bodhisattva enters into immeasurable cycles of beginning and end without weariness or aversion;
whereas the Śrāvaka loathes the various hardships of birth,
the Bodhisattva undergoes birth without such afflictions.
The śrāvaka feels weary and disenchanted with the work of merit;
the bodhisattva accumulates manifold virtues without ever feeling weary or satisfied, nor does he encounter distress.
The śrāvaka loathes being amidst a great assembly.
The Bodhisattva transforms and edifies the multitudes of sentient beings without being deterred by hardships;
whereas the Śrāvaka feels revulsion toward prefectures, kingdoms, counties, and towns,
the Bodhisattva enters universally into prefectures, kingdoms, counties, towns, provinces, and great nations without being weary of their evils.
Śrāvakas loathe their own bodies and worldly afflictions;
Bodhisattvas, however, do not suffer from the desires and afflictions of all sentient beings.
Indeed, Śāriputra!
"What the families of the śrāvakas find loathsome and repulsive, the bodhisattva mahāsattva encounters no distress or difficulty regarding.
Chapter Five: The Eight Powers. Thereupon, Śāriputra asked the Jewel Woman:
"By what power does the bodhisattva mahāsattva encounter nothing loathsome or repulsive?"
The Jewel Maiden replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva possesses eight powers that are free from weariness or distaste."
What are the eight?
First is the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which refrains from inflicting harm.
Second is the power of compassion (*karuṇā*), which does not abandon the multitude of beings.
The third is the power of harmony, which does not become inferior.
The fourth is the power of wisdom, which is free from worldly afflictions.
The fifth is the power of capability, whose mind never experiences weariness.
Sixth is the power of virtue, which acts without attachment.
Seventh is the power of the sages, which is free from folly and stupidity.
Eighth is the power of progress, whose fundamental intent is the supreme vow.
"These are the eight powers.
They are established by the Bodhisattva as he moves through the world; by the power of his virtue and wisdom, he never feels weariness or aversion.
The Elder Śāriputra then asked the Jewel Woman:
"Do you possess such power as this, that you can come and go and move about with equanimity?
The Jewel Maiden replied,
"If one abides in equanimity through equanimity, and is able to practice all forms of equanimity in this way, then one possesses neither power nor weakness."
That which is equanimity neither exists nor does it not exist; there is no non-existence, no creation, and no practice of what is created—this is called equanimity.

Equanimity is like space; all phenomena are likewise like space. That which is like space has no space; that which is empty and void is called quiescence, being beyond verbal expression, like a vast wilderness. All phenomena are likewise thus!
"Just as space is vast and formless, and likewise beyond words, so too this equanimity is neither weak nor powerful.
Indeed, Śāriputra!"
When a bodhisattva is weak and inferior, they possess power. Why is this?
If one is weakened by afflictions and sensual desires, then through wisdom one possesses power and influence.
If one is weak due to stinginess and greed, one employs generosity to achieve strength.
If one is weak due to the violation of precepts, one achieves strength through the observance of the precepts!
If one is weak and inferior due to anger and hatred, then patience shall be one's power and authority!
If one is weak and inferior due to indolence, then diligence shall be one's power and authority!
If one regards a distracted mind as weak and inferior, then one regards meditative concentration as power and influence!
If one regards false wisdom as weak and inferior, then one regards right wisdom as power and influence!
"Regarding all these dharmas, even if a bodhisattva is weak and inferior in unwholesome virtues, they shall nevertheless possess the power and influence of the roots of virtue!
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Jewel Maiden, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"If you wish to speak, you should say this.
When these words were spoken, five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).
Chapter Six: The Ten Powers. The Jewel Woman addressed the Buddha:
"What are these so-called ten powers of the Tathāgata? By what powers are they constituted such that they are fully accomplished?
The Buddha told the Jewel Maiden:

"Suppose a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path; never having turned toward the establishment of the inferior vehicle, he ultimately never commits unwholesome karma. It is by means of this firm power that he proceeds to the site of enlightenment."
The Jewel Maiden asked again:
"What are the ten powers?
The Buddha told the Jewel Maiden:
"Power reaches every place; by the power of reaching every place, one knows things as they truly are;
one knows with certainty whether things are finite or infinite.
Suppose, Jewel Woman!"
The Tathāgata knows, with precise certainty, that which is "everywhere" and "not everywhere," as well as the finite and the infinite; this is the first power of the Tathāgata.

By means of this, the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, expounding the essential teaching of non-attachment and turning the pure Wheel of Dharma. Among śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, Māras, Brahmās, and worldly beings, none can withstand his majestic virtue, for he always acts in accordance with the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one desires that there be no remaining retribution for past calamities, sins, or merits. By virtue of having attained the power of compliant cultivation, they reach the realization of the Buddha-way and fully know the origins of all sins and merits of the past, future, and present."

If the Tathāgata knows the retributions for offenses and blessings in the past, future, and present, and discerns with certainty the destinations of good and evil, this constitutes the second power of the Tathāgata.

The power of the Tathāgata issues forth as a lion’s roar within the assembly; he explains the state of non-attachment and turns the pure wheel of Dharma. Among śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, Māras, Brahmās, and worldly beings, none can withstand his majestic virtue!
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

One who practices the bodhisattva path observes the faculties of sentient beings and preaches the Dharma for them; having understood their origins, one delivers them. If one acts in accordance with the faculties of all people, one thereby fulfills the requirements to attain the Buddha-way. For the sake of all sentient beings, one uses the faculty of diligence to discern and understand the multitudes exactly as they are."
"Suppose, Jewel Woman!
The Tathāgata, knowing the fundamental roots of all beings as they truly are, utters the lion's roar; this is the third power of the Tathāgata, for it accords with the Dharma."
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one enters the realms of sentient beings and the categories of persons, establishing them according to the inclinations of each individual and in accordance with the masses. Through the ultimate power of entering these realms, one attains the Buddha-way and understands the countless forms and various types of bodies within the world."
If the Tathāgata enters the realm of sentient beings and guides each according to their faith and joy, this is the fourth power of the Tathāgata, for it accords with the Dharma.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, if the various classes of sentient beings desire liberation, they shall be encouraged and rescued according to their respective inclinations. Seeking wisdom and vision, one perceives them with compassionate faith and without revulsion or loathing. Through this power of faith and liberation, one ultimately achieves the state of Buddhahood, knowing the manifold inclinations of the masses and discerning their immeasurable joys as they truly are."
"Suppose, Jewel Woman!
The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the various kinds of faith of sages and sentient beings, and he knows with precision their immeasurable inclinations; this is the fifth power of the Tathāgata."
Yet, amidst the multitude, he lets out the lion’s roar; as for śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, Māras, and Brahmās, none can withstand his sublime and majestic virtue!
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one manifests and dispatches wisdom regarding all dharmas—whether conditioned or unconditioned, with form or formless. Whether seeking the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the Great Vehicle, through the power of this perfected wisdom, one attains the Buddha-way and enters entirely into ultimate wisdom, knowing things exactly as they are."
"Suppose, Jewel Maiden!
The Tathāgata universally enters into all wisdoms, reaching everywhere without exception and knowing things as they truly are.
He walks alone amidst the multitude and roars the lion’s roar; his towering virtues in the heavens and the world can be matched by none, and he always acts in accordance with the Dharma."
This is the sixth power of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!
One who practices the bodhisattva path never abandons or loses the roots of virtue from the past, nor does one become negligent regarding the transcendence of their original vows."

By means of this power of not forgetting the fundamental virtues of antiquity, he fulfills and perfects them until attaining the path of Buddhahood; he recollects the events of incalculable kalpas in the past, knowing them with exact precision as they truly were.
"Suppose, Jewel Woman!

The Tathāgata, knowing his own past and that of other sentient beings throughout incalculable eons, recollects them all with perfect sincerity and knows them as if they were present; and he utters the lion’s roar before the great assembly—this is the seventh power."
No śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, Māras, or Brahmās can withstand him!
This is because he always acts in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, O Ratnā, daughter of noble family!

Practicing the bodhisattva path, they cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), samādhi, and right reception (*samāpatti*) with a mind free from arising; detached from the dust of desire, they are disciplined, serene, gentle, and benevolent.
By the power of this gentleness and benevolence, they fulfill all perfections and attain the Buddha-way.

She has thoroughly understood all the meditative reflections, gates of liberation, concentrations, and states of meditative attainment of the common people, as well as their afflictions and fetters, knowing them exactly as they are.
Suppose, O Jewel Woman!

The Tathāgata clearly understands all the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and right attainments of sentient beings, as well as their afflictions and fetters, knowing them exactly as they are; this is the eighth power of the Tathāgata.
Yet, amidst the great assembly, his lion’s roar—unassailable by śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, Māras, or Brahmās—is such that none can withstand its majestic virtue!
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one never conceals the merits of sentient beings; one does not slight those who have not yet studied nor treat with arrogance those who are inferior, thereby attaining manifest clarity that illuminates all sentient beings."

By means of this vast and magnificent radiance, he will ultimately attain full perfection and realize the path of Buddhahood; with the divine eye, he will see through all things and know them as they truly are.
Suppose, O Ratnā, daughter!
The Tathāgata’s eye of the path of truth penetrates all things, seeing everything without exception; this is the ninth power of the Tathāgata.
He wanders alone among the great assemblies and roars the lion's roar; as for śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, Māras, and Brahmās, none can withstand his majestic and sublime virtue!
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one does not lead sentient beings toward tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*). Rather, one preaches the Dharma for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) to the masses so as not to increase their outflows, and seeks the path of no-outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*) for the sake of sentient beings to reveal the correct way."

Through the power of their mutual, untainted, and profound faith, they shall fully perfect the ultimate attainment of the Buddha-way; they will universally reach all things through wisdom that has exhausted all outflows, knowing them exactly as they are.
Furthermore, Jewel Woman!
If the Tathāgata, having exhausted all outflows, reveals all-outflow-free wisdom, this is the tenth power of the Tathāgata.

When the Tathāgata, having attained such true power, utters the lion’s roar amidst the assembly, he turns the pure wheel of Dharma without any point of attachment; no śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, Māras, Brahmās, or worldly beings are able to withstand him!
This, O Ratnā, is the tenfold power of the Tathāgata.
It is because the Tathāgata has fully accomplished these ten powers that he may be called perfectly awakened.
"If a bodhisattva hears of this power, by means of these ten powers of a bodhisattva, they shall achieve the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
Chapter Seven: The Four Fearlessnesses. The Jewel Woman addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are these what are called the four fearlessnesses of the supreme Tathāgata and the eighteen unique qualities of all Buddhas?"

Furthermore, by what practices does that bodhisattva attain the four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? The World-Honored One replied: “Practicing the bodhisattva path, he never violates or disregards the instructions of his teachers.

Understanding these characteristics, he always regards sentient beings with an impartial mind. He gives away all that he possesses without stinginess, equally upholds and practices the Dharma, and observes its ultimate destination. Free from manifold conceptualizations, he remains detached from all attachments. As soon as he attains the Way of the Buddha, he lets out a lion’s roar: ‘I have realized the attainment of equal enlightenment.’”
"You should know this: I have fully understood these dharmas, such that there is nothing I have not awakened to and mastered.

Even if there were śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, Māras, Brahmās, or worldly people who could not perceive the Tathāgata’s auspicious response, his profound elegance, and his majestic radiance."

Even if one were unable to perceive his manifest and responsive virtues and sought to find faults in the Buddha, failing to see any at all, one might still dare to give rise to such thoughts, thinking to oneself:
"The Buddha has not attained equal and perfect enlightenment."

"Should anyone say this, [they would be wrong for] the Buddha is without fear and his conduct is fearless; he strides alone amidst the great assembly and roars the lion's roar. Knowing the state of non-attachment, he turns the pure wheel of Dharma. Among śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, Māras, Brahmās, and worldly people, none can withstand his majestic virtue!"
This is the first fearlessness of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, O Ratnāvalī!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one knows internal conduct and distinguishes between internal and external phenomena; furthermore, one clearly understands obstructive dharmas, neither practicing nor following regressive dharmas, neither complying with them nor acting upon them oneself, neither transforming others through them nor proclaiming them. Upon seeing all such obstructions, one completely abandons them.

Upon attaining the Way of Buddhahood, he utters the Lion’s Roar, never again seeing any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, nāga, yakṣa, māra-king, Brahmā, or other worldly beings who would argue or dispute, saying:
"The Tathāgata teaches a doctrine of obstruction and causes people to practice it."

"Although such words exist, he does not feel fear; practicing without dread, he turns the great wheel of Dharma amidst the great assembly and roars the lion's roar—this is the Tathāgata’s second fearlessness."

"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden! One who practices the Bodhisattva path constantly upholds the pure and white Dharma; they expound the sutras along paths free from contention and dispute, purifying all classes of sentient beings. They take refuge now in transcendent virtues and the karma of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) which bears countless burdens. Thus, they universally attain entry into the purification of fetters and resentments, personally accumulating the karma of the unconditioned. This is the source of the Buddha’s transformation of the masses; upon attaining the Way of the Buddha, he lets out the lion's roar. By means of purifying all fetters and resentments, I preach the Dharma and cultivate this practice, thereby attaining complete adornment and purity."
Never shall one see a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a Māra, a Brahmā, or any other person in the world who could rightfully argue, saying:
"The Tathāgata has taught a doctrine of harboring resentment."

"Although these words exist, he does not feel fear; practicing without dread, he turns the Great Wheel of Dharma amidst the great assembly and roars the lion's roar—this is the third fearlessness of the Tathāgata."
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!
When practicing the bodhisattva path, one never dwells in extreme arrogance, thinking: 'I have knowledge and I have vision, whereas others have neither knowledge nor vision.'"
His resolve is always humble and he is not conceited; he awakens to all matters and does not cling to unwholesome conduct.

By following this Dharma and bringing it entirely to fulfillment, he shall attain the Way of the Buddha and let out the lion’s roar, saying: "You should know that my body has exhausted all outflows (āsravas), and thus I have eliminated the afflictions of birth and death."
Furthermore, he extensively expounds the sutras for the sake of sentient beings to eliminate all outflows (*āsrava*).
Never shall any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, nāga, yakṣa, Māra, Brahmā, or other worldly beings find grounds to accuse him, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s preaching does not eliminate the outflows; his outflows are not yet exhausted."

"Although such words exist, he does not feel fear; practicing without dread, he turns the Great Wheel of Dharma amidst the great assembly and roars the lion's roar—this is the fourth fearlessness of the Tathāgata."
