Chapter Eight: The Eighteen Unshared Dharmas Furthermore, O Ratnāvalī!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, for all sentient beings who have constantly lost their way, one shall guide them by showing the paths—whether they be ditches, pits, treacherous terrain, elevations, depressions, or deviant tracks—and shall level them to make them even while establishing bridges. In dark places and remote, desolate lands, one shall then establish Buddhist temples that are lofty, vast, and exceedingly magnificent.

Suppose there were a person who, while dwelling amidst the guilt of doubt, acts for the sake of countless classes of sentient beings, clearing away their hesitant guilt so that they do not fall into calamity but find a place of rest, and furthermore, does not give rise to the doubts of others.

One does not speak of others' shortcomings or say that someone has committed a transgression; one understands the infinite dispositions of sentient beings and eliminates all their worldly aspirations and practices. One preaches the Dharma without doubt or hesitation, thereby manifesting the great radiance of the Dharma and bestowing the light of great wisdom. One encourages all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to preach the sutras, bestowing the grace of the Dharma-gift without flattery or deceit. One establishes wholesome karma and exhorts others to do the same, never disparaging others nor engaging in jesting or frivolous play. One does not inflict harm nor speak in derision; regarding the customs of various lands, one remains free from arrogance. In all speech, one places sole trust in the words of the Buddha.

Attaining mastery by following the teachings of written words, they know that words are empty; regarding all matters expressed through speech, they perceive no flaws or impurities, seek out no shortcomings, and do not look for any deficiencies.
If a bodhisattva practices such dharmas and attains the path of Buddhahood, this is called being without flaw or defect.
Being without flaw or defect, one is then able to fulfill all-encompassing wisdom.

If there are questions regarding matters that require analytical explanation, they penetrate them all without exception and illuminate them universally; they have skillfully cultivated samādhi and are adept at clear understanding; they enter entirely into the dhāraṇī of all sounds and constantly extol the flawless words of the Tathāgata while preaching the Dharma; yet in all these, they do not create anything within the realm of letters. This, O Jewel Maiden, is what it means.
This is the foremost unique quality of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Jewel Woman, one who practices the bodhisattva path abandons all evil speech of the mouth;

whatever they say is ultimate sincerity, rooted in the Dharma and centered on reasoned discourse. With edification as their vocation, they do not engage in falsehood or cause harm. They completely relinquish the speech of those who are not noble ones and cultivate the tranquil conduct of the noble ones. Free from contention and dispute, they accord with the principles established by the śramaṇas.
If one hears the sutras, seeks out their meaning, and explains them for others—all this is for the sake of oneself and others. One aspires to the practice of the meditative absorption of cessation;

never does one engage in conflict, harbor resentment, or seek legal redress. One does not pursue verbal disputes nor cling to emptiness; by believing and understanding the practice of emptiness, one becomes free from attachment. One crosses over the names and titles of dharmas, placing steadfast faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding the path of non-action. One exhorts and transforms other people and classes of sentient beings, causing them to enter this Dharma. Having followed this Dharma, one attains the Buddha-way; this is called being without dispute or contention.
He is without sound; he does not employ words through a single syllable, nor is there anything he speaks.
He does not abide in any karmic activities, yet he exhorts and transforms others in this True Dharma.
Having cultivated this Dharma and attained the path of Buddhahood, there is no verbal expression.
Because there is no sound or speech, nothing is expounded through even a single syllable; nor is there anything taught, nor any worldly activity.
For the sake of those gathered in the assembly, he skillfully expounds the principles of the Dharma in a manner that accords with the minds of the multitude;

his speech and words are harmonious and timely, moving the entire realm. Having well cultivated samādhi, he clearly discerns and understands immeasurable practices and the gates of dhāraṇī. Thus, in accordance with all the seasonal rhythms and endowed with every mark and every excellence of a Tathāgata, from every pore he produces the immeasurable and inconceivable sounds of the Buddha-dharma. With the sound emanated from even a single hair, he can fully describe and gladden the hearts of all those in the assembly, preaching the gates of immeasurable dharmas; these sounds emerge spontaneously, brought about by the power established through his original vows in the past.
The Tathāgata has no conceptual thoughts regarding that; he is eternally tranquil and seeks nothing through action. This is the second unique quality of the Tathāgata, not shared with other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

One who practices the Bodhisattva path never fails or loses the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). They constantly recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, recollect the Saṅgha, and possess the recollection of the devas; they recollect the practice of giving and recollect the practice of wisdom, and they also transform others, causing them to practice these six recollections."

Having practiced this Dharma, they attain the Way of Buddhahood; they never lose their resolve as they rescue and mindfully protect sentient beings, attaining mastery over all dharmas, skillfully cultivating samādhi, and clearly discerning and understanding the dhāraṇī of the Lamp of Dharma.
Furthermore, the Honored Tathāgata is fully mindful of all phenomena and never forgets them.
At that time, by means of his unprecedented conduct, he perceives the thoughts and intentions of all classes of sentient beings.
When those who wish to come and ask questions [approach], the Tathāgata fully understands them and no longer needs to reflect; if there are those who inquire, he explains them for them.

Such speech is characterized by a mind that is clear and penetrating, free from all obstructions, and is able to skillfully expound the teachings to delight the minds of the assembly. With a single word, in a single moment, he reaches everyone completely. This is the third unique quality of the Tathāgata, not shared with other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!
When practicing the bodhisattva path, one should always protect the minds of others, not allowing other people to give rise to anger or resentment;
one should not cause their minds to be disturbed, nor distress the hearts of others, nor cause their minds to become foul."
They never obstruct or neglect the roots of virtue in others, nor do they sever the Dharma, but rather believe in their own minds.

Like a magical illusion, they are without thought or perception and do not act with self-indulgence; they maintain an impartial mind toward all classes of sentient beings, equally contemplate all phenomena within the single Dharma-realm, and enter into that which is indestructible.

Having practiced this Dharma and attained the path of Buddhahood, one then achieves constant concentration, such that there is not even a moment when the mind is not concentrated. One contemplates all dharmas as entirely spontaneous; this is called the Samādhi of Equal Accumulation.

Furthermore, he skillfully discerns the universal gate dhāraṇī; the Tathāgata is constantly in meditative concentration, manifesting all the deeds of the Buddhas without any disparate activity—this is the fourth unshared quality of the Tathāgata among all Buddhas.

"Furthermore, Jewel Woman! When practicing the bodhisattva path, one is free from inverted perceptions and thoughts; the mind does not act perversely, does not create false views, and does not engage in falsehood. Thus, one does not conceive of a self or a body. There is no perception of a person (*pudgala*), nor a perception of a life-span (*jīva*), nor a perception of a soul (*jantu*). There is no perception of a man (*puruṣa*), nor a perception of a human being (*manuja*), nor a perception of one who trains (*śaikṣa*), nor a perception of cessation, nor a perception of permanence, nor any perception of views. There is no perception of the three realms, nor even the thought of being detached from the three realms.

Furthermore, there is neither good nor evil, neither fault nor faultlessness, neither outflow (*āsrava*) nor non-outflow, neither the mundane nor the supramundane. Having eradicated the roots of affliction, there is no perception of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) or nirvāṇa, nor any perception of gathering or assembly."

The inclinations, natures, and thoughts of sentient beings are inverted; once these have been eliminated, they cultivate various virtues. Thus, they distance themselves from the perceptions of ordinary worldlings, cast off all erroneous views, and moreover, without relying on anything in between, they contemplate the Dharma of equality.
Having practiced this Dharma, he attains the path of Buddhahood without any manifold thoughts; this is called the Tathāgata being forever free from all conceptualizations.

He is thus able to skillfully cultivate the Samādhi of Non-conceptualization and understands the gate of the Dhāraṇī of the Inexhaustible Treasury. As the Tathāgata wanders and walks about, he is without thought, yet he gives rise to great compassion for all sentient beings who harbor false imaginings. For those among the masses who are bound by attachments to practices, he exhorts, transforms, and teaches them according to the proper timing. This is the fifth unique quality of the Tathāgata, not shared with other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one should constantly observe with the mind those who wander through birth and death. Having examined the various dharmas of worldly toil and affliction, one then guides and leads them to universal peace, establishing them in the contemplation of the Dharma so that they no longer grieve and all suffering is extinguished."
Not being anxious in the pursuit of various gains, one eliminates the fetters of longing;
nor does one greedily crave the benefits obtained through all forms of offerings, so that even if those gains are lost, one does not suffer from the fetter of grief.
One contemplates that all myriad things are entirely impermanent and are nothing but suffering;
without regarding the phenomena of the body, one places faith in the tranquility of Nirvana, while simultaneously observing the multitude of sentient beings.

Observing all phenomena through such forms and images, one practices and attains mastery in following and cultivating this Dharma; when one ultimately fulfills it and reaches the path of Buddhahood, it is called "Unobstructed."

That which cannot be calculated or conceptualized through observation is the Tathāgata’s unified proclamation of the well-cultivated samādhi, named "Detached from the Three Contemplations," which brings clear understanding of the ocean-seal dhāraṇī of the conditioned.

The Tathāgata universally serves all devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, humans, and non-humans; all provide offerings to the Buddha and serve him without fail. He does not grow weary of this, nor does he become attached to it. When followers of various heterodox paths, externalists with their wondrous arts, or beings who violate the precepts come to disturb him, he feels no sorrow or distress. His mind is equanimous, having realized that all things are ultimately non-existent; his mind is equanimous because there is nothing at all.
Just as the earth endures all things without exception;
just as water washes away all impurities and turbidity;
and just as fire burns everything without exception; so too is the mind.
If the mind is like the wind, universally unattached and free from longing;
if the mind is like space, likewise free from resentment;

if one treats all sentient beings with an impartial mind, observing the practice of tranquility within this Dharma, contemplating and examining the conduct of human beings, and being fully endowed with what is observed while constantly giving rise to great compassion; if one enters among sentient beings to deliver those who need no delivering, transforming the multitudes without missing the proper timing, preaching the Dharma according to the fundamental conduct of individuals, remaining neither wavering nor indolent—this is the sixth unique quality of the Tathāgata, not shared by others.

"Furthermore, Jewel Woman! One who practices the bodhisattva path diligently eliminates all evils and cultivates practice with earnestness, seeking all dharmas of virtuous merit. They take delight in the subtle and find boundless joy in them; they rejoice in the various kinds of most profound roots of goodness. They cast aside the matters of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, setting their will upon the Mahāyāna without ever regressing. They give rise to great compassion for sentient beings, contemplating the true meaning without ever forgetting or abandoning it. Having eliminated the notion of a self for the sake of others, they gather together all the dharmas of the Buddhas."

Because he delights in the Dharma through these means, he cannot abandon his aspiration for the Buddha-way; seeing that the hosts of Māras rely on perversity and turn toward false views, he therefore accumulates the True Dharma for their sake. Upon attaining the Buddha-way, he is thus called the Tathāgata who does not lose the joy of the True Dharma.

By being able to skillfully follow the samādhi of one's own preference, they discern and clearly understand the vajra-dhāraṇī, and with mastery over the Dharma, they preach that which should be expounded.

In every direction, at once and in a mere moment, whenever he returns to any time or place and possesses anything, he teaches the Dharma according to the dispositions and natures of sentient beings as they are vessels for the Dharma, each following their own conduct; he never deviates from the concentration of samādhi. This is the seventh unique quality of the Tathāgata, not shared with other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman! One who practices the bodhisattva path always exerts diligence;

never abandoning or distancing oneself from the roots of goodness, one never tires of them; gathering together appropriate virtues without neglecting or violating them; honoring all beings and respecting spiritual friends; approaching Dharma masters, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas to attend upon them, consult them, and receive their teachings; serving and following them with immeasurable diligence; traveling through countless lands to protect those in the cycle of birth and death; and liberating infinite classes of sentient beings."

They purify immeasurable Buddha-lands, make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones; they grasp and uphold the teachings of immeasurable Buddhas, realize the noble wisdom of immeasurable Buddhas, enter into the conduct of immeasurable sentient beings, and clearly understand the immeasurable methods for expounding the Dharma.

Because he encourages others through this Dharma, he ultimately fulfills all requirements and attains the Way of the Buddha; this is called "not losing diligence. The Tathāgata’s diligence is never lost;

he has skillfully cultivated this practice of diligence, as well as samādhi, meditative concentration, and the transformations of the *ṛddhipāda*. The Tathāgata’s spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) and transformations are immeasurable and manifest in extraordinary ways, converting and liberating countless beings. With firm sincerity and unobstructed freedom from the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), he travels through all buddha-fields without diminution or effort, yet pervades the entirety of space. This is the eighth unique quality of the Tathāgata, not shared with other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one’s mind should always be single-mindedly focused on the foremost resolve; moreover, one should constantly remain composed and fully perfect the mind of ultimate truth, never forgetting any mundane or supramundane dharmas, and diligently practice the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness."
He then observes the conduct of his own internal body, focusing exclusively on the matters of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
he further observes the external body, seeing that the activities of the body are the practices of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
and he observes both the internal and external body as matters of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Contemplating internal sensations, one sees that sensations are empty, and thus practices with single-minded dedication;
contemplating external sensations, one sees that sensations are empty;
contemplating both internal and external sensations, one contemplates and realizes that internal and external sensations are empty.
Observing the activity of the internal mind, one sees that the internal mind contemplates only non-conceptualization;
observing the external mind, one sees that the activity of the external mind is focused solely on signlessness;
observing both the internal and external minds, one sees that both the internal and external minds are focused solely on signlessness.
Contemplating internal phenomena, one perceives that in the practice of internal phenomena there is no aspiration;
contemplating external phenomena, one perceives that in external phenomena there is exclusively the thought of non-aspiration;
contemplating both internal and external phenomena, one perceives that in the practice of both internal and external phenomena there is the thought of non-aspiration.

He attains the four foundations of mindfulness regarding the body, contemplating it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; he fully accomplishes the body of a Tathāgata without severing the wholesome virtues of the body, and by understanding sensations, he attains the foundations of mindfulness.

Contemplating emptiness and observing all things, one causes the multitudes of beings in the various realms of existence to find rest; by establishing great compassion for all those in evil destinies to eliminate their suffering and afflictions, the mind attains liberation and penetration—this is called the application of mindfulness of the mind (*manasikāra*).

To cultivate exclusively the signless while not contravening or losing the bodhisattva-mind, accumulating and practicing the deeds of the Mahāyāna without indolence or abandonment, and for the mind to take refuge in the Dharma—this is called *smṛtyupasthāna* (the foundations of mindfulness).

To cultivate the wishless (apraṇihita) exclusively, yet not to realize it within the state of desirelessness; to contemplate the Buddha-dharma and enter the immeasurable dharma-realm with equanimity; and having cultivated this dharma to ultimate penetration and realization, to attain the path of Buddhahood—this is called "not losing the intent for the Way."

The Tathāgata is eternally in a state of meditative concentration, his resolve never forgotten; he eliminates all conditioned activities and skillfully cultivates samādhi. The Tathāgata expounds upon the matters of transformation, perceiving the thoughts and mental inclinations of all sentient beings across the past, future, and present, as well as their faith, understanding, and faculties. He delivers them from the conduct of worldly toil and craving, clearly comprehending the attachments arising from the causes and conditions of fetters, and the karmic retributions of non-virtuous deeds, as well as the cycle of birth and death with its merits and transgressions from beginning to end.
Knowing the assemblies of śrāvakas in all buddha-fields, and understanding the time when bodhisattvas practice their conduct and receive their predictions of enlightenment;

he speaks of his own parents, kinsmen, relatives, and friends, his mental faculties being clear and penetrating so that he never forgets them, and his explanations regarding the eight stations of consciousness are without a single falsehood—this is the ninth unique quality of a Tathāgata, not shared by others.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

One who practices the bodhisattva path always adheres to wisdom—the radiance of wisdom, the majestic brilliance of wisdom, and the manifest discernment of wisdom. It proclaims the light of the lamp of knowledge and the sagely understanding of the noble ones; its profound and wondrous clarity, its wisdom that brings wearying detachment from desire, is beyond analogy. The wisdom thus aroused reaches all things, such that it cannot be surpassed by the wisdom of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."

He possesses a wisdom that has never before existed—a vast, profound, and boundless wisdom; a wisdom that transcends the ordinary; a wisdom realized after emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation; and a wisdom of mindfulness that dwells nowhere and clings to nothing. He seeks out learning without weariness, is intent upon noble realization, and having fully mastered extensive knowledge, he returns to ultimate wisdom.

Beholding the world as if one's head were on fire, they ardently aspire to the wisdom of the Great Vehicle; whatever they hear is like the great ocean, for they are able to discern and analyze what they have heard.

They take delight in the sūtras and find joy in the bliss of the Dharma; seeking the Dharma, they practice diligence. Because this bliss of the Dharma is formless and beyond categorization, they relinquish everything internal and external without any stinginess. With humble and respectful minds, they honor their elders and teachers, constantly receiving their instructions.

Regarding the suffering of the five aggregates, there is none they cannot endure; they completely renounce all comforts and pleasures, finding joy instead in the diligent pursuit of the sublime Dharma.

Hearing a single four-line verse, they would not value it at even a full thousand pieces of gold; they would rather wish to hear a single phrase of the Dharma than aspire to obtain the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
They vow to seek the Perfection of Hearing with joyful longing, having no greed for attaining the rank of Śakra or Brahmā.

It would be better to joyfully preach even a four-line verse for others as a gift of Dharma than to rely upon performing vast sacrifices and offerings on a scale equal to the sands of the Ganges for all who are in want;
it would be better to joyfully exhort others to resolve upon the path of enlightenment than to attain the status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King on a scale equal to the sands of the Ganges;

it would be better to joyfully lecture on the sutras for others, expounding the practices of the Infinite Deliverance (Pāramitā) to be followed, than to obtain the nature and conduct of Śakra or Brahmā Kings on a scale equal to the sands of the Ganges.

Thus, for one who has achieved such single-minded devotion to hearing the sutras and explains them to others with a focused mind, there are few who can equal their diligent practice and observance of what they have received.
He is revered and honored by all the devas and is held in the thoughts of all Buddhas; he is protected by the guardianship of the devas.

Once the Buddhas have turned their attention toward him, the secular classics and the sublime sūtras that transcend the world appear spontaneously. Without study, he attains complete mastery and reaches the light of inexhaustible wisdom.
Having practiced these dharmas to ultimate perfection and attained the Way of the Buddha, he is therefore called the Tathāgata.

Possessing unshared wisdom and the noble realization of the True Dharma, his brilliance is sublime and unimpeded, free from the hindrances of the skandhas. He fully knows the mental activities and thoughts of all sentient beings—their good and evil inclinations, their destinations; whether they have speech or are silent, whether they have transgressions or are blameless, whether they are with outflows or without outflows; and he distinguishes and explains for them all things: the mundane and the supramundane, worldly afflictions and resentment, birth-and-death, and nirvāṇa.

They enter into all dharma-gates, awakening to and clearly understanding them through recitation; they know the matters of the past, future, and present with wisdom as clear as the dust motes filling all lands, without any obstruction or hindrance.

He fully understands all such kalpas without any obstruction, clearly comprehending the limits of the past and the future; he explains the boundless reaches of the past and future worlds, entering into the examination of consciousness and conduct, and skillfully cultivating samādhi and teaching through transformations.

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, by means of a single dharma-gate, is able to discern all dharma-gates, causing one dharma-gate to enter into all dharma-gates; this is the tenth unique quality of the Buddhas, not shared by others.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!
One who practices the bodhisattva path never aspires to or yearns for the household life.

Nor does one delight in leaving the household, yet one manifests the practice of renunciation and training, becoming a śramaṇa who delights in tranquility, regarding stillness as supreme and silence as one's vocation. One cultivates and practices the profound and wondrous Dharma of diligence, and furthermore upholds these three gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."

None of the various Māras or external adversaries dare to confront them; none of the various inverted views or heterodox perspectives can transgress against them, as they transform all classes of sentient beings who are attached to conceptualizations.

He then focuses his practice exclusively on these three gates of liberation, thereby attaining the gate of unobstructed liberation. Spontaneously, the light of unhindered wisdom arises within him; he transcends the realm of Māra and fulfills the noble realm, no longer practicing any of the aggregates of obscuration, nor the inverted coverings, the dwellings in false views, the dust of affliction, or the manifold conceptualizations.

He then clearly understands the gateway of the absence of hindrances (anīvaraṇa) and finds delight in the three gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha). He then analytically expounds the profound Dharma, adhering solely to the essential meaning rather than ornamental rhetoric;
adhering solely to essential wisdom rather than consciousness (vijñāna);
and adhering to the analytical essentials rather than prolixity.
One should take refuge only in the Dharma and not in persons.

That which one takes refuge in guides and benefits all sentient beings; with elegant and refined language, it transcends all conceptual associations, explaining and analyzing until one returns to the essential meaning and attains liberation.
Regarding the conceptualization of form, one provides explanations and analysis, leading them to essential wisdom for their deliverance; though there be many words, they are brought into harmony!
One speaks of the equality of form, causing them to return to the correct teaching for their deliverance!
Relying upon assemblies of people, he discriminates and exhorts them to lead them back to the Dharma and deliver them!
Even if an assembly consists of those with the sixty-two views, he explains for them the essentials of non-arising and non-extinction to enable their deliverance!
If one dwells amidst the delusions caused by all conceptualizations, one liberates them by means of the signless (animitta) and delivers them!
If one dwells within the three realms, one liberates them by means of the wishless (apraṇihita) and delivers them!
For those gathered in the practice of desire, deliver them through the liberation of emptiness and purity!
For those gathered in hatred, deliver them by discerning the mind of loving-kindness!
For those who frequent the conduct of folly, deliver them by explaining the twelvefold linkage of dependent origination!
Entering into assemblies of those who are greedy, he skillfully analyzes and teaches them the Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā) to deliver them;
among the multitude who violate prohibitions, he skillfully analyzes and teaches them the Perfection of Precepts (Śīlapāramitā) to deliver them.
Among those who harbor anger and hatred, he analytically explains and teaches the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) to deliver them!
Among those who are indolent, he analytically explains and teaches the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) to deliver them!
Among those with distracted minds, he analytically manifests and teaches the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) to deliver them;
among those with false wisdom, he analytically manifests and teaches the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to deliver them!
Among the multitudes of ordinary beings, he delivers them by analytically expounding the discourse on the Noble Truths!
Among the multitudes of those with the four inversions, he delivers them by analytically expounding the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self!
Amidst the multitude obscured by all the hindrances and veils, and deluded by inverted and false views, he analyzes and explains the gate of liberation free from hindrances, thereby delivering them!
Among the masses of worldly afflictions, he manifests and expounds the dharmas of the stages of the path of the Buddhas of the ten directions to deliver and liberate them!
Having practiced these dharmas until they are ultimately perfected, he attains the Way of the Buddha; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata who does not fail to deliver and liberate.

Because they do not lose their liberation, they are free from anger; having reached the ultimate root source without deficiency, they are pure and cool from beginning to end as they traverse all realms of existence. They enter into the profound and wondrous divine wisdom they have attained, which is unassailable and exceedingly difficult to withstand!
Surpassing the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, one can walk alone upon the path of all Buddhas.

Free from defilement and stainless, one is without blemish; ultimately pure, one is adorned and refined. With the karma of tranquil contemplation, one’s resolve is such that it can be explained as inexhaustible, immeasurable, and boundless. Thus, within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no obstruction; practicing with equanimity like space, one skillfully cultivates the samādhi called the "Stainless Treasury" (*Vimalagarbha*).
It illuminates all phenomena, bringing full clarity to the *dhāraṇīs*; the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is entirely free from conceptualization.

For all who come to him for refuge and approach him, he universally radiates light to bring about great illumination. He inclines toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), venerates extinction (*nirvāṇa*), and reaches the ultimate limit of the most profound *parinirvāṇa*. This is the eleventh unique quality of the Buddhas, not shared by others.

"Furthermore, O Ratnāvatī! When practicing the bodhisattva path, one takes wisdom as supreme and wisdom as one's power; one returns to essential wisdom and discourses on the land of wisdom. Transcending all that various wisdoms lead toward, one adorns and purifies the noble path and manifests its practice. Seeking transcendence and distinction, one cultivates and purifies the supernormal powers to achieve all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). By cultivating the resolve for the path to its ultimate fulfillment, one attains noble penetration and reaches all-encompassing wisdom."
If there is a mind of desire, one knows the arising of the mind of desire; if there is no mind of desire, one knows the arising of the mind free from desire.
If there is a mind of hatred, one knows the arising of the mind of hatred; if one is free from a mind of hatred, one knows the arising of the mind free from hatred.
If there is a mind of delusion, one knows the arising of the mind of delusion; if one is free from a mind of delusion, one knows the arising of the mind free from delusion.
If there is a mind of affliction (*kleśa*), one knows the arising of that mind of affliction; if there is a mind free from affliction, one knows the arising of that mind free from affliction.
If there is a mind of sleepiness, one knows the arising of that mind of sleepiness; if there is a mind free from sleepiness, one knows the arising of that mind free from sleepiness.
If there is a mind of attachment, one knows the arising of that mind of attachment; if there is a mind free from attachment, one knows the arising of that mind free from attachment.

If one aspires to cultivate the mind, one knows the arising of the aspiration to cultivate the mind; if one is free from the aspiration to cultivate the mind, one knows the arising of being free from the aspiration to cultivate the mind.

If one covets the minds of others, one knows the arising of the covetousness for the minds of others; if one is free from coveting the minds of others, one knows the arising of being free from the covetousness for the minds of others.
If one has a surpassable mind, one knows the arising of the surpassable mind; if one has an unsurpassable mind, one knows the arising of the unsurpassable mind.
If the mind is covered by hindrances, one knows that the mind has arisen with hindrances; if the mind is free from hindrances, one knows that the mind has arisen free from hindrances.
If there is no resolute mind, one knows that the mind has arisen without resolution; if there is a resolute mind, one knows that the mind has arisen with resolution.
If there is an evil mind, one knows that an evil mind has arisen; if there is a mind of virtuous merit, one knows that a mind of virtuous merit has arisen.
If there is a mind with defilements, he knows the arising of that mind with defilements; if there is a mind free from defilements, he knows the arising of that mind free from defilements;

if there is a mind subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), he knows the arising of that mind subject to outflows; if there is a mind free from outflows (*anāsrava*), he knows the arising of that mind free from outflows;
if there is a mundane mind, he knows the arising of that mundane mind; if there is a supramundane mind, he knows the arising of that supramundane mind.
If there is a mind of attachment, one knows the arising of that mind of attachment; if there is a mind free from attachment, one knows the arising of that mind free from attachment;
if there is a pure mind, one knows the arising of that pure mind;
if there is a meager mind, one knows the arising of that meager mind.
If there is a distracted mind, he knows the arising of that distracted mind;
if there is a concentrated mind, he knows the arising of that concentrated mind; if there is a mind free from contact, he knows the arising of that mind free from contact;
if there is a limited mind, he knows the arising of that limited mind; if there is an unlimited mind, he knows the arising of that unlimited mind.
To state the essentials: whether it be a mind of stinginess and greed or a mind of giving;
a mind that transgresses prohibitions or a mind that upholds the precepts;
or a mind of anger and resentment or a mind of patience.
Whether it be a mind of indolence or a mind of diligence;
whether it be a mind of distracted thought or a mind of meditative concentration;
whether it be a mind of false wisdom or a mind of the perfection of right wisdom;
The minds of ordinary beings and the minds of sages;
minds tending toward false views and minds tending toward right views;
the mind of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the mind of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the mind of the Mahāyāna, or the mind that clearly understands the Great Way.

"Furthermore, knowing that which arises from the cause of the Truth of Suffering is the Truth of Origination; this Truth of the Cessation of Suffering is the cessation itself; and for one who proceeds toward the Path, there is the Truth of the Way, known as it truly is."

Having already been able to comprehend the Truth of Suffering as it truly is, one knows that the primordial purity of wisdom has no arising, and that the ultimate wisdom of the beginning and end is beyond cultivation.

One knows the Truth of Suffering exactly as it is: there is nothing to be severed, nor is there any faith [in its cessation], for it is eternally and completely exhausted. One comprehends the path such that all enter into it universally, yet governs it with equanimity like space, being without self and without craving.

Furthermore, that locus is fundamentally and entirely pure; they all thoroughly understand the source of these Four Noble Truths, and having examined them through existence and non-existence, they realize there is nothing to be constructed or proven. Thus, they transform sentient beings, eliminate their [false] vows regarding the truths, and practice in accordance with clear realization.

If one preaches the Dharma for the sake of the masses, attaining true gentleness and compliance through that teaching, and remaining unconfused and undisturbed regarding dependent origination; if one casts aside all various heterodox and divergent views and dwells in the entry into the Middle Way to contemplate the law of causes and conditions, then one thoroughly understands all phenomena and the conditions of retribution. One does not abide in the land of self, nor in the land of others; one does not abide in the land of longevity, nor in the land of life; nor, furthermore, does one abide in the land of sentient beings.

One knows that ignorance leads to these volitional formations; one knows that from volitional formations arises consciousness; one knows that from consciousness arises name-and-form; one knows that conditioned by name-and-form arise the six sense bases; one knows that conditioned by the six sense bases arises contact; one knows that conditioned by contact arise feelings; one knows that conditioned by feelings arises craving; one knows that conditioned by craving arises grasping; one knows that conditioned by grasping arises becoming; one knows that conditioned by becoming arises birth; and one knows that conditioned by birth arise old age, death, lamentation, sorrow, grief, and the affliction of suffering.
Through such causes and conditions, one brings about the great aggregate of the body.

Fully comprehending emptiness, ignorance is exhausted; thus, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age, sickness, death, weeping, lamentation, and sorrow—the great aggregate of the body is forever extinguished!

"He forms this contemplation that the condition of ignorance has no self as its condition, nor does it have another person as its condition; it has no life-force, no vitality, and no sentient being as its condition.
If there is no self, no person, no life-force, and no sentient being, then this is emptiness."
One who already knows emptiness does not reckon it as permanent, nor do they reckon it as subject to annihilation; they do not even reckon it as impermanent, much less as annihilated.
Thus, regarding the past, there is nothing produced and nothing arisen.
If one establishes that in the past there is nothing produced and nothing arisen, then one will have no attachment to the three periods of time.
Having no attachment to the three periods of time, one attains nothing at all; thus, non-existence is the natural state!

That which is already devoid of anything existing and is naturally quiescent has transcended the paths of coming and going; one who has been able to transcend the paths of coming and going possesses the foremost deliberation, and by means of this foremost deliberation, it is called "correct and true."

"Having already attained the true words of that Buddha, one who has the true words of the Buddha has no contention; having no contention, one’s will is set upon the Dharma; and with the will set upon the Dharma, one is naturally like space."

From this wise practice, one comes to understand it clearly: by practicing what is non-conforming, one cultivates ignorance; through the cultivation of ignorance, there arise volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), clinging (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, sickness, death, lamentation, grief, and despair—the accumulation of this great mass of suffering. Thus, the afflictions of bodily distress are not eliminated, yet one thoroughly investigates and understands all the views upon which they depend, seeing how they are formed through the convergence of causes, conditions, and karmic retribution.

Having already been able to discern that there is no self and no person, no life-force and no individuality, all phenomena are naturally such that they do not undergo limits; neither are they not so, nor is there anything to be attained.
If one cannot grasp the limit, then there is no root or source; once the root and source are absent, one beholds the central mean.
If one cannot grasp the root and source of all phenomena, by what cause could there be a central mean therein?
What kind of things constitute that which is "correct" therein?

By means of transcending the infinite dharmas of correctness, one becomes free from the dharmas of this, that, or the middle; thus, one is able to expound the essentials of immeasurable, central, and correct sūtras. Because those who can practice such dharmas ultimately attain fulfillment and reach the path of Buddhahood, they are therefore called the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One.

"He shall never fail or impair the wisdom of transcendent knowledge and insight; provided he does not fail or impair the wisdom of transcendent knowledge and insight, by means of that wisdom of transcendent knowledge and insight, he will immediately be able to practice the samādhi of power and progress, clearly comprehend immeasurable sovereign dhāraṇīs, and thereby govern the infinite, central realm of reality (dharmadhātu) with equanimity."

Just as space is devoid of conceptual thought, he then expounds the wisdom of formless karma; distinguishing karmic retributions without any forgetfulness, he eloquently elucidates the equality of past, future, and present events.

He directly observes the inclinations of the faculties of all sentient beings and explains the understanding of their diligence and wisdom; he discerns and resolves the infinite bodies and incalculable forms, praising and expounding upon worldly conduct while skillfully establishing the teaching of inexhaustible matters. He proclaims and manifests immeasurable faith, further distinguishing and explaining various types of faith, and thoroughly penetrating all internal divisions in every direction to resolve limitless difficulties. Regarding all spheres of activity, he speaks of the wisdom of advancing and retreating, unfolding inconceivable gateways to all dharmas, and proclaiming all dhyānas, doors of liberation, samādhis, and correct meditative attainments.

The desires of worldly toil and the knots of anger structure the destinies of all beings from beginning to end; he fully understands the intermediate states between good and evil. Possessing the wisdom that is free from the five hindrances throughout countless past eons, he universally manifests immeasurable and diverse transformations, and he recollects all the events of ancient times.

“Furthermore, they observe all things without exception, fully comprehending and proclaiming the immeasurable and the unobstructed. With the divine eye that penetrates all, they explain everything without leaving any hindrance remaining; having attained liberation and eliminated all obstructive wisdom, they have exhausted all outflows and possess the ear of wisdom!”
Having established that there is nothing whatsoever, the wisdom of fearlessness is taught as being entirely without distinction; it is equal like a scale, never ceasing its Buddha-activities.

It teaches the wisdom of the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), preaching the Dharma in accordance with the original conduct of beings. It extols all dharmas as having no fixed location, transforming and enlightening sentient beings by turning the wheel of Dharma. Possessing a wisdom free from indolence or partiality, it proclaims the profound and various differences [of phenomena], transcending the abyss to reach a transformation that is ever more vast. Moved by the power of wisdom, this is something that cannot be reached by the vehicles of any *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*; these are the twelve unique qualities of the Tathāgata, the dharmas not shared with other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman! When practicing the bodhisattva path and undertaking noble deeds, one does not seek renown.

Thus, by means of one's own person, one undertakes the work of wisdom; one no longer engages in any bodily impurity, flattery, or deception. One is free from harmful conduct and free from acts of stinginess and greed, constantly cultivating the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Through physical diligence, one acts in accordance with the Way, neither causing affliction to oneself nor oppressing others. Relying on the *pāramitās*, one practices great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), always making it the focus of one’s bodily cultivation for the sake of sentient beings."

If one is fully endowed with these, and practices according to this Dharma in such a manner as to attain the path of Buddhahood, this is called the Tathāgata’s mastery over the virtues and wisdom of bodily conduct.

Through the body, they realize the clarity of all-encompassing wisdom; having attained equal mastery, they behold all forms and are able to manifest all manner of colors through samādhi, clearly understanding and universally entering the essentials of dhāraṇī.

The Tathāgata has manifested countless forms, appearing in various kinds of images and countenances: all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, brahmins, gentlemen, elders, householders, farmers, artisans, craftsmen, commoners, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

Furthermore, an incalculable and immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of people all came and sat together in assembly. The Buddha manifested immeasurable dignified deportment and ritual propriety; his countenance and physical form were most venerable, supreme, foremost, and that of a Great Man, possessing immeasurable rectitude. He preached the Dharma for the assembly, exhorting, transforming, dispatching, and inspiring many toward progress. Midway through, he vanished from their sight, suddenly disappearing, whereupon the multitude attained understanding.

Therefore, the great assembly gathers together, sitting side by side to discuss and deliberate with mutual joy. The wisdom they expound is tranquil as they walk in meditation; those who behold them never grow weary of it, and those who hear their teachings are filled with exultation. Their minds attain such delight that they no longer seek ordinary worldly joy. Regarding all sensual pleasures, realms, wealth, and undertakings—even if these were to vanish and disappear, there would be none who did not look up to them with longing thirst. Desiring to attend upon them and hear the recitation of the scriptures, even those who possess attachments to desire or views of affectionate love, upon hearing the Dharma preached, will take pleasure in receiving it. Through this karmic response, they reach the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*); their body, speech, and mind become stabilized and free from blemish. To attain such conduct and practice is the thirteenth of the Tathāgata’s unique qualities not shared with other Buddhas.

"Furthermore, O Jewel Maiden! One who practices the bodhisattva path and performs the deeds of noble wisdom does not seek fame or renown; whatever is spoken from their mouth promotes only matters of wisdom. They are not deluded by any defects, evils, flattery, or sycophancy; their speech is sincere and free from double-tonguedness, and they avoid coarse words. They do not slander others, but their speech is gentle and smooth, never employing harsh discourse, and whenever they speak, they invariably preach the Dharma."
That which is proclaimed from his mouth causes neither himself nor others to harbor distress or feverish agitation;
that which is spoken from his mouth accords with the Buddha’s Dharma and leads toward what is wholesome;

the words spoken from his mouth accord with the hearts of sentient beings, causing no injury, and his wisdom remains serene and composed; his speech is perfect and complete, yet he does not pursue fame.
By bringing these practices to ultimate fulfillment, one attains the Buddha-way; this is called the Tathāgata’s mastery over the wisdom and virtue of speech that is equal [to all].

Through this mastery over the wisdom and virtue of speech that is equal to all, he skillfully cultivates the samādhi of the Jewel-Action (*ratnakārya*), attains the three grades of comprehension, and masters the dhāraṇīs. That which the Tathāgata enters by means of a single utterance and a single dharma-word universally penetrates all things; he proclaims all sounds, equally gladdening the hearts of all those in the assembly.

Every sound uttered by the Tathāgata accords with reason and does not contravene the principles of the Dharma; it is characterized by utmost sincerity and gentleness, observes the law of causes and conditions, eliminates all defilements, and is free from craving and desire. Having attained tranquil concentration, he shall surely realize the fruition of sincerity, even unto Nirvāṇa. This is the fourteenth of the unique qualities of a Buddha, not shared by others.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, even if one constantly cultivates the karma of wisdom, one does not seek fame or sensory form. By contemplating with the mind that which is aroused by noble wisdom, one causes sentient beings to leave behind faults, evils, attachments, and the matters of wicked flattery, ignorance, anger, and inverted views."

Abiding in and practicing right view with compassion, one treats all commoners with an impartial mind and does not abandon the resolve for the Way. Having fully perfected the cultivation of wisdom, one is neither arrogant nor self-indulgent. By practicing this Dharma, one attains the path of Buddhahood; this is what is meant by the Tathāgata’s mental intention: the diligent cultivation of noble wisdom, the thorough realization of one’s aspirations, and the sovereign mastery of the noble clarity of mind and wisdom.

Having attained this, he possesses the noble mastery of all wisdom and mind; he has well-cultivated the samādhi that manifests before the eyes of all present Buddhas, and he maintains the dhāraṇī of pure mindfulness, which is lucid and pristine.

The Tathāgata, with a single mind, universally knows the mental activities of all sentient beings; because his mind is already equanimous, he is able to be universally equal toward all the masses. By exhorting and assisting others with a mind that is level and equal to all, he is able to equalize those whom he exhorts and assists. His mind is like an illusion, pure by nature; all minds are naturally like space.

The Way-dharma equally governs the bodily, verbal, and mental activities of all sentient beings; by means of the dharma of sentient beings, it enters one's own body. All the bodies through which the Way-dharma is cultivated are like manifested reflections. If one can equally govern all these bodies with wisdom, then all sentient beings enter into one's own body.

Because he is able to equally govern all bodies and cause them to enter his own body, in the mere instant of a thought, he causes the bodies of sentient beings to be transformed and established as the Buddha-body.

This establishment cannot be destroyed; it cannot be shaken, nor can it be transferred by anyone in the heavens or the world—neither by gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, nor Brahmas—who are unable to advance or retreat against it. This is the fifteenth unique quality of the Tathāgata, a dharma not shared with other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Maiden!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one hears of the unimpeded wisdom of the past Tathāgatas, the Arhats; that all these Perfectly Enlightened Ones pervade all worlds universally, being without obstruction or hindrance, and one develops firm faith in the conduct, deeds, and modes of deportment of their bodies."

The sounds of all worlds are fundamentally quiescent; there are none that do not enter into the infinite, inexhaustible, and inconceivable voices of the Buddhas, which analyze and expound immeasurable Dharma-gates.

The words of all these past Tathāgatas are non-dual; so too it is with the Buddhas and Perfectly Awakened Ones in the lands of the ten directions, their various authentic scriptures, all common people, and all Bodhisattvas.

He thoroughly understands the causes and conditions of merit and demerit, as well as the thoughts and actions of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all other people; he further possesses profound faith in the mental conduct of past Tathāgatas, whose radiant light is pure, immeasurable, and free from all obscurations.
Those who believe in these past Tathāgatas harbor no doubt nor any hesitation; they are neither terrified, nor afraid, nor do they feel apprehension. The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable.

Understanding sentient beings in such a manner, they cause them all to delight in all dharmas and encourage their assistance; by practicing this Dharma until it is ultimately perfected, they attain the Buddha-way. This is called the sovereign manifestation of the immeasurable and unimpaired wisdom of the Tathāgata regarding the past.

"By means of his sovereign wisdom regarding the past, he further skillfully cultivates the samādhi of the 'Valiant Subjugation,' clearly discerning and understanding the *dhāraṇī* of Radiant Splendor. He knows the various distinct names and the limits of the lifespans of the multitude of Tathāgatas of the past; within that, through his boundless wisdom, he is able to exhaustively reach the very source of their origins. It is the same for the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past."

Regarding the actions performed by the various classes of sentient beings, and the good and evil deeds, blessings and calamities cultivated by people—just as there have been all the kalpas of the past, by which kalpa does one achieve perfect enlightenment and awaken those who are not yet awakened?
"In a certain eon, how many Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appeared?
These Tathāgatas also, within that eon, expounded the source that is immeasurable, unimpeded, and beyond all limit or exhaustion."

Furthermore, one comprehends that the worlds of the Buddhas of the past each have distinct names—whether they be defiled or pure, numerous or few, large or small, subtle or exquisite—and the locations where they enter according to the limits of afflictions; just as they correspond to their respective places throughout the ten directions, they are distinguished by diamond nets and entered through the realms of the nets of the various faculties. All these past [realms] are without limit; the boundaries of the Buddha-lands cannot be fully reached.

The Tathāgata has universally expounded all of this; he never forgets these past events and is fully able to resolve and comprehend the wisdom of all Buddhas, just as a person looks at their own palm and sees the five fingers!
These are the sixteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata, not shared by other Buddhas.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!
One who practices the bodhisattva path hears that the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is without obstruction."

These Perfectly Enlightened Ones universally traverse all worlds; their bodies are infinite and free from the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha*). All the movements of their bodies, their majestic deportment, and their ritual propriety are fully trusted and revered, and their voices reach far and wide, pervading everywhere without exception.

In all Buddha-lands, they hear the teachings of the Dharma and thereby enter the infinite gateways of the Dharma that have been expounded; they place faith in the words of future Tathāgatas regarding the retribution for the merits and demerits, virtues and evils, committed by the Buddhas and Perfectly Awakened Ones of the lands in the ten directions, as well as by all sentient beings, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings.

Furthermore, they believe and know the destination of the minds of all future Buddhas—their radiance, majestic spiritual power, and purity being infinite and free from the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-āvaraṇa*). Believing in the conduct of these future Buddhas, they harbor no doubt nor any hesitation; they are neither terrified nor afraid, nor do they feel any difficulty, as they possess firm faith in the inconceivable realm of the Buddhas.

Then, once again, for the sake of all sentient beings, he exhorts and assists them to gather [merit]; thus, he thoroughly expounds such teachings of the Dharma and brings forth faith and joy. Having practiced this Dharma until it is ultimately perfected, he attains the Way of the Buddha; this is called the Tathāgata’s future, incalculable, and unfailing mastery over manifest wisdom.

"By means of his future wisdom that is free from impairment, having manifested mastery, he then gives rise to the samādhi of the power of great compassion and clearly discerns the dhāraṇī of the Lion’s Thunderous Roar. Thus, he is able to know the various distinct names and the lifespans of future Buddhas; within this, he explains them boundlessly and inexhaustibly, attaining their very source."

Furthermore, he cognizes the future conduct of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the multitudes of sentient beings, as well as the karmic retributions of fortune and calamity that the populace shall encounter;
he also knows all future kalpas, and in which kalpa he shall attain perfect enlightenment and awaken those who have not yet awakened.

Furthermore, regarding the intermediate eons he traversed, they are without limit and cannot be exhausted; their origins are such that the names of future worlds—whether defiled or pure, numerous or few, large or small, subtle or exquisite—are as infinite as the number of motes of dust. The Tathāgata knows them all without omission or forgetfulness, and through his compliant conduct throughout the ten directions, he is able to universally enter every portion of those networks of origins within the countless Buddha-worlds of the future.
All these Tathāgatas explain this in detail; they observe it as clearly as one views the five fingers upon the palm of one's own hand!
This is the seventeenth unique quality of the Buddhas, not shared by others.
"Furthermore, Jewel Woman!

When practicing the bodhisattva path, one hears of the unhindered wisdom of all present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas; their manifest enlightenment, whose bodies are infinite and free from the hindrances of the aggregates (skandha-āvaraṇa); the spheres of activity of the Buddhas, the deeds performed by their bodies, and the deportment and etiquette of their physical movements;

as well as their voices, which pervade all lands without obstruction or concealment, and through which they faithfully explain the inconceivable sounds of the Buddhas and the immeasurable gateways to the path of all dharmas."

They faithfully accept and delight in all the words spoken by the Tathāgatas currently present; they discern and distinguish the true awakening of the Buddhas in the lands of the ten directions, as well as their various sūtras, and all the multitudes of sentient beings, including bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all people.

The mental activities of these Tathāgatas, the luminous purity of the deeds they initiate, are incalculable and free from all obscurations; they all further believe in these present Tathāgatas, harboring no doubt and having no impediments, neither fearing nor being afraid, nor even trembling, for the realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable.

Furthermore, he exhorts and transforms other sentient beings so that they likewise believe in and delight in these scriptural teachings; when their practice of the Dharma is thus perfected and brought to completion, they attain the path of Buddhahood. This is called the Tathāgata’s present, infinite, and undiminished mastery over manifest wisdom.

"Because he has manifested mastery through the unimpaired wisdom of the countless Tathāgatas of the present, he has skillfully cultivated the samādhi of the Seal of Stainless Illumination and thoroughly understands and discerns the dhāraṇī of the Vajra Maṇḍala."

The Tathāgata, being present, is universally able to discern the names of all Buddhas, each distinct from the others; he can fully proclaim the limits of their lifespans, which are utterly isolated in the interim and without boundary, such that they cannot be exhausted and their ultimate source cannot be reached.
The present conduct of all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and sentient beings; the activities of all living creatures and the retributions for their merits and transgressions;
the number of kalpas currently existing throughout the ten directions, and the attainment of perfect enlightenment within those kalpas—their origins are explained.

The present lands throughout the ten directions, each having its own name, whether mixed or pure, numerous or few, large or small, soft or subtle—all are universally entered. According to the limits of atoms and in accordance with what is appropriate, the networks of the faculties in all locations throughout the ten directions are entirely entered into the present worlds of the ten directions. Within these, there are infinite boundaries that cannot be exhausted, yet their origins are fully attained.

In that regard, the Tathāgata’s analytical discourse suffers no diminution; this discerning wisdom of all Tathāgatas is like observing one's own palm and examining its five fingers—this is the eighteenth unique quality of the Buddhas, the *āveṇika-dharma* of the Tathāgatas.
“By means of these eighteen categories, one attains all the dharmas unique to the Buddhas.
What are the dharmas unique to the Buddhas?
That no one is able to see the mark of the Tathāgata’s crown is a dharma unique to the Buddhas, because his body is limitless.”
The Tathāgata transcends all forms; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for he is the most honored among all people.
When sentient beings behold the Buddha, their defilements are eliminated; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for his body is like medicine.
The conduct of the Tathāgata is sublime, exquisite, and transcendent; this is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, for it is free from transgression.
The Tathāgata is fearless; this is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, for he has attained fearlessness.
The Tathāgata walks alone; being free from all outflows (āsrava) and having attained mastery, this is an unshared quality of the Buddhas, for he abides in equanimity.

The mental conduct of the Tathāgata is indestructible; this is an unshared quality of the Buddhas, for he thoroughly understands the instructions of the noble ones (ārya). The Tathāgata’s will is disciplined, settled, and serene; this is an unshared quality of the Buddhas, for he is firmly established in his own practice.
The Tathāgata’s eloquence responds in accordance with the occasion; this is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, for he expounds the sūtras without relying on verbal instruction.

The Tathāgata can gladden the minds and thoughts of all sentient beings; for this reason he is called "Tathāgata," and this is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, for there is nothing further to be attained.

The Tathāgata’s voice is heard throughout the assembly without overflowing beyond it; this is an unshared quality of the Buddhas. He expounds the Dharma without falsehood, transforming and guiding those ready for liberation, and rescuing their faculties to bring them to full maturity.

That all the assemblies in the place of enlightenment personally approach and behold the countenance of the Tathāgata is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for his transformations and spiritual movements are inconceivable.
To behold the Tathāgata without ever becoming weary or satiated is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for the body of the Great Sage is like a great and boundless tree of precious jewels.
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is free from any partiality or injustice; this is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, because of their perfectly equal awakening.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be scrutinized; this is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, because his dignified deportment and ritual etiquette are free from any expectation of reward.
The body of the Tathāgata walks with the gait of a lion; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for he has no hesitation amidst the great assembly.
The Tathāgata’s stride is free from falsehood; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for his wisdom constitutes the very basis of the actions he performs.
The Tathāgata’s practice of the true reality of sounds is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for his wisdom is supreme and his speech is true.
The Tathāgata’s eye surveys all without limit; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for his noble wisdom is foremost and his mind is clear and penetrating.
The Tathāgata’s eloquent instructions are radiant and brilliant; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, because he possesses instantaneous and decisive eloquence.
The Tathāgata’s gains, offerings, and fame overflow; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, because his unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment is inexhaustible.
The merit of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, because it is the foremost discernment that fully comprehends all obstacles.

He has become a Tathāgata whom none can withstand; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, because he possesses the body of a Mahānagna wrestler, endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, being the foremost and supreme among the pāramitās.
The Tathāgata is never weary and never regresses; his teaching is tireless. This is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, for he thoroughly understands the faculties of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata acts as the holy teacher for countless dharmas; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for he alone is the universally honored teacher throughout all worlds.
His lifespan is immeasurable; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, because he manifests the Dharma-body.

Those who behold the Tathāgata or hear his voice, and who draw near to him and prostrate before him, find no falsehood therein; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for when those who have investigated the beginning and end prostrate in worship, it immediately causes sentient beings to reach great peace.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is free from fetters and resentment; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, because he understands the equality of the three periods of time.
The Tathāgata’s discourse has no interval; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, because it accords with the fundamental nature of phenomena.
The Tathāgata has eliminated all hindrances; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for all unwholesome dharmas have been forever eradicated without remainder.
The Tathāgata has no teacher; this is an uncommon quality of the Buddhas, for he has spontaneously realized all dharmas by himself.
The Tathāgata’s universal wisdom is an uncommon quality of all Buddhas, for it discerns all forms of awakening and fully comprehends the Great Way without exception.
This constitutes the attainment of all the uncommon qualities of all Buddhas.
