Chapter Nine: The Thirty-two Marks.
At that time, the Jewel Woman addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, Great Sage!"

Regarding these thirty-two marks of a great man that are now called those of the Tathāgata, the Most True One—what merits did he practice in his previous lives and destinies such that he attained these thirty-two marks of a great man, which are now spread across his body?
The Buddha told the Jewel Woman:
"In ages past, I practiced immeasurable virtues and accumulated various deeds; by means of this, the Tathāgata has attained the thirty-two marks of a great man, which are spread across my body."
Now, to briefly set forth the essentials:

as for the mark of a Great Man, the Tathāgata’s feet standing level upon the ground, this is because in ages past he firmly encouraged and assisted others without ever turning back, and never concealed the merits of others.
The Tathāgata’s hands and feet possess the mark of a great man with wheels because in ages past he established various kinds of giving.

The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, possesses the mark of a great man with long, slender, and beautiful fingers because in ages past he expounded the meaning of the sutras to protect sentient beings and cause them to be free from suffering.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, consisting of webbed hands and feet, is due to his never having caused the separation of others' families in past ages.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, consisting of soft and exquisite hands and feet, is due to his having given various kinds of fine and delicate garments as gifts in past ages.
That the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a great man characterized by seven parts being full and rounded is because, in ages long past, he extensively provided various gifts to supply those in need.

That the Tathāgata’s knees are level and without joints, and his calves are like those of a deer, is because, in ages long past, he received and upheld the scriptures without ever violating or losing them.

The Tathāgata’s body possesses the mark of a great man known as the sheathed male organ because, in ages past, he was scrupulous regarding his own person and remained far removed from the ways of desire.

The Tathāgata’s body possesses the mark of a great man known as the fullness of the jaw, like that of a lion, because, in ages past, he extensively cultivated pure deeds and perfected his spiritual practice.
As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man, the *svastika* that naturally appears upon his chest, it is because in ages past he eliminated all defilement, turbidity, and unwholesome conduct.
That the Tathāgata’s limbs are fully endowed with the marks of a great man is because, in ages past, he bestowed fearlessness and comforted others.
That the Tathāgata’s arms extend below his knees, a mark of a great man, is because, in ages past, when people had tasks to perform, he assisted and encouraged them.
The Tathāgata’s body is pure and free from blemish; this mark of a great man is because in ages past he practiced the ten wholesome paths of action without weariness.

The Tathāgata’s crown of the head is full and well-proportioned; this mark of a great man is because in ages past, when there were those who were ill, he attended to them and treated them with various kinds of medicine.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of lion-like strides is due to having fully cultivated and perfected many roots of virtue in past ages.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of forty white teeth is due to having been benevolent in nature toward sentient beings in past ages.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of teeth without gaps: this is because in ages long past, he brought together those who were disputing and quarreling.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of prominent jaw-teeth: this is because in ages long past, he gave gifts of subtle, exquisite, and pleasing objects.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of pure, white, and beautiful hair and eyebrows is due to having well protected his own body, speech, and mind in ages long past.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of a broad and long tongue is due to having spoken with utmost sincerity and guarded against verbal transgressions in ages long past.

The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man characterized by a serene countenance results from having cultivated a mind of ultimate benevolence and harmony through the offering of immeasurable merit, thereby fulfilling the vows of sentient beings and providing them with shelter.

The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice, like the cry of the sorrowful pheasant, is a mark of a Great Man resulting from his having, in ages past, spoken with gentleness; he spoke to all people while guarding his mouth and moderating his words, so that there were no numberless persons who did not rejoice upon hearing what he said.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of sapphire-blue pupils is due to his having constantly observed all people with eyes of compassion throughout past ages.

The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of eyes like the newly risen moon is due to his having been free from coarse and violent intent, and possessing a nature that was harmonious and gentle, throughout past ages.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows resulted from his having, in ages past, praised and sung of the virtues of those dwelling in seclusion.

The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of the natural fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head resulted from his having, in ages past, reverently served the worthy and holy ones and paid homage to his elders.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of soft and exquisite skin is due to his having, in ages past, gathered the treasury of the Dharma with every thought.
The Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of a body the color of purple-polished gold is due to his having, in ages past, frequently given clothing, bedding, and seats.
That each hair on the Tathāgata’s body grows singly as a mark of a Great Man is because, in ages past, he remained aloof from assemblies and the clamor of crowds.

That the hairs on the Tathāgata’s body curl upward to the right as a mark of a Great Man is because, in ages past, he revered his teachers, received the instructions of virtuous friends, and followed them with prostrations.

As for the Tathāgata’s mark of a great man consisting of hair that is deep blue-black in color: this is because in ages long past, out of compassion for the masses of living beings, he did not inflict harm upon them with weapons or staffs.

The Tathāgata’s body is perfectly square and circular, free from any curvature; this mark of a Great Man arises because in past ages he exhorted and settled sentient beings, causing them to abide in a concentrated mind.

The Tathāgata’s spine is like a great chain of hooks; this mark of a Great Man, characterized by universal majesty and towering virtue, arose because in past ages he established images for all the Perfectly Awakened Ones, restored ruined temples, exhorted those who were estranged to reconcile, bestowed fearlessness upon others, and transformed those engaged in disputes so that they would act in harmony.

Daughter, if you wish to know this: in my past lives, I practiced the roots of immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of virtues. It was by practicing in such a manner throughout my previous existences that the Tathāgata was able to attain these thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
At that time, the Jewel Woman addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“It is truly unprecedented, O God among Gods!
The roots of virtue cultivated by the Tathāgata in the past are indeed beyond compare, as he analytically expounds the Dharma of all Buddhas.”
The Buddha told the Jewel Woman: "So it is, so it is!
Just as you have said, the Tathāgata indeed analyzes and explains the Dharma of all Buddhas."

If there are bodhisattvas who attain the hearing of these roots of virtue planted by the Tathāgatas in the past and expounded by all Buddhas, they shall obtain infinite and supreme blessings; they will immediately take refuge in the practice of the True Dharma and will be able to fully perfect all the teachings of the Buddhas.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma-gate chapter on the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the thirty-two marks of a great man, the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways, and a magnificent radiance shone everywhere throughout the Buddha-lands. Immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
twenty-five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
In the void of space, hundreds of thousands of celestial beings rained down heavenly flowers and played celestial music—lutes, flutes, pipes, and zithers—raising their voices in praise, saying:

"Should there be any among the multitude who hear of these ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; who, being fully endowed with merit and free from fault, believe and rejoice without doubt, and practice according to the aforementioned teachings, they shall then, before this great assembly and before the world of gods and men, utter the lion’s roar, just as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does today, uttering the lion’s roar before gods and men."

Why is this so? This true scripture does not ultimately lead to those of inferior disposition or meager faith who stand at the head of the multitude of followers of the Hīnayāna; rather, it shall lead to those who follow the pure Dharma. When such a person attains the essentials of this scripture, they will love, revere, and find it pleasing, rejoicing with leaping joy.
Chapter Ten: On the Practice of Dharma. At that time, the Jewel Woman addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How truly marvelous, O God among Gods!"
The Tathāgata has thus expounded the true scriptures of all Buddhas, which are the roots of merit from all past ages.
World-Honored One,
what are the scriptures that a bodhisattva practices and cultivates called, such that they constitute the practice of the Dharma?
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas.
The Buddha told the Jewel Maiden:
"Purity of intention and disposition is the practice of a bodhisattva;
having steadfast friends is a practice;
and being one who acts with reciprocity is a practice."
To be able to cultivate the practice of bestowing grace is the practice of the Dharma;
to be able to endure verbal abuse is the practice of the Dharma;
furthermore, not abandoning those who take refuge is the practice of the Dharma.
For one who is weak and inferior, to be able to practice patience is the practice of the Dharma;
for that which is difficult to provide, to be able to give it away is the practice of the Dharma;
to have compassion for all beings is the practice of the Dharma.
To have a nature of compassion is the practice of the Dharma;
to protect those who violate the precepts is the practice of the Dharma;
to contemplate the sutras is the practice of the Dharma.
To accord with and follow the Way of the Teachings is to practice the Dharma;
to delight in and cherish the authentic scriptures is to practice the Dharma;
to guide and master the various sutras is to practice the Dharma.
To accord with profound stillness is the practice of the Dharma;
to delight in solitude is the practice of the Dharma;
and to never tire of dwelling in seclusion is the practice of the Dharma.
To remain in seclusion is the practice of the Dharma;
to withdraw from the assembly is the practice of the Dharma;
to protect sentient beings is the practice of the Dharma.
To perceive nothing that can be diminished is the practice of the Dharma;
to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness exclusively is the practice of the Dharma;
to enter into great compassion is the practice of the Dharma.
To delight in and love the Dharma is the practice of the Dharma;
to contemplate meditative concentration is the practice of the Dharma;
to arouse and manifest the mind of enlightenment is the practice of the Dharma.
To praise the Mahāyāna Dharma is the practice;
to cast off the heavy burden is the practice;
for the mind not to be timid or weak is the practice.
To contemplate contentment is the practice of the Dharma;
to cast aside greed, excess, and the stinginess of desire is the practice of the Dharma;
to know moderation and the virtue of the noble ones' sufficiency, while remaining sparing in speech, is the practice of the Dharma.
To be free from contention, strife, discord, resentment, and malice, and to practice patience and benevolence, is the practice of the Dharma;
to have faith and knowledge regarding the retribution of the karma of sin and merit is the practice of the Dharma;
and to follow the seven riches—faith, precepts, learning, generosity, shame, dread of blame, and wisdom—is the practice of the Dharma.
To honor and respect one's elders, to follow and obey virtuous friends, and to receive instructions with reverent courtesy, is the practice of the Dharma;
to maintain a mind that is always humble, respectful, compliant, and self-effacing, is the practice of the Dharma;
not to disparage oneself, not to revile others, not to boast of one's own virtues, and not to conceal the merits of others, is the practice of the Dharma.
To eliminate worldly desires and cast aside anger, folly, and delusion; to be free from arrogance—this is the practice of the Dharma.
To be fully endowed with the observance of majestic deportment and ritual propriety—this is the practice of the Dharma.
To listen well to the sūtras with joy and gladness—this is the practice of the Dharma.
Not to be separated from the Buddha, to have firm faith in the true scriptures, and to reverently follow the noble Sangha—this is the practice of the Dharma;
to practice generosity, to discipline the mind, to possess wisdom, and to leave the household life to purely cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya)—this is the practice of the Dharma;
to remain unshaken by gain or loss, praise or blame, fame or insignificance, or suffering or pleasure, thereby transcending all worldly dharmas—this is the practice of the Dharma.
If, upon seeing friends, relatives, or enemies, one greets them with a face of harmony and joy, free from sorrow or dejection, this is the practice of the Dharma;

if one is free from frivolity, remains aloof from darkness and ignorance, is without flattery, does not act with depravity, and is without blemish, such that one’s fundamental nature is ultimately pure from beginning to end, this is the practice of the Dharma;

and if one practices the four debts of gratitude, bestows gifts, acts with kindness and love, and benefits others through impartial benefit, gathering all together to rescue and deliver sentient beings, this is the practice of the Dharma.
To practice the dharma of steadfastness is to practice the Dharma;

to recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Noble Sangha; to reflect upon giving, reflect upon observing the precepts, and reflect upon the devas—these are the practices of the Dharma;
and the perfections of giving, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom—these perfections are the practices of the Dharma.
To use skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to encourage and assist the root of all virtues for the sake of bodhisattvas is the practice of the Dharma;
to purify body, speech, and mind while guarding the ten wholesome paths is the practice of the Dharma;

and to have faith and understanding that things are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, being without a person, without a self, without a life-principle, and without a vital soul—this is the practice of the Dharma.
To discern emptiness, establish non-conceptualization, and clearly understand wishlessness, remaining unattached within the triple world—this is the practice of the Dharma.

To practice the foundations of mindfulness and the right efforts, to cultivate the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment, thereby entering the path and contemplating tranquility—this is the practice of the Dharma.
The Buddha told the Jewel Woman:
"One who practices the Dharma is said to have neither eyes nor the activity of the eyes, and no mental activity of forms;
neither ears nor the activity of sounds, and no mental activity of echoes."
There is no activity of the nose nor any activity regarding odors, nor is there any conceptualization of the activity regarding odors;
there is no activity of the tongue nor any activity regarding tastes, nor is there any conceptualization of the activity regarding tastes;
there is no activity of the body nor any activity regarding the tactile, nor is there any conceptualization of the tactile.

To have no mental activity regarding forms and no activity regarding phenomena, not to conceptualize activity regarding phenomena, and to have no activity regarding form—this is the practice of the Dharma.

To have no conceptualization of form, no conceptualization of suffering regarding form, no activity regarding a self in form, and no activity regarding the non-quiescence of form—this is the practice of the Dharma.
To have no activity regarding the emptiness of form, and no activity regarding the non-conceptualization of what is not form—this is the practice of the Dharma.
It is not the practice of wishlessness regarding form;
it is not the practice of non-activity regarding form;
nor is it the practice of tranquility regarding form; nor is it the practice of purity regarding form.
Furthermore, it is not a form characterized by the practice of investigation;
furthermore, it is not a form characterized by the practice of non-arising;
furthermore, it is not a form characterized by the practice of non-origination.
Furthermore, it is not a practice of non-attachment to form;
nor is it the ultimate practice regarding form;
nor is it a practice based on the absence of an origin in form—this is the practice of the Dharma.
In this way, the formations of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness constitute the practice of formations.

It is not the practice of the impermanence of consciousness, nor the practice of the suffering of consciousness, nor the practice of the non-self of consciousness, nor the practice of the stillness of consciousness, nor the practice of the emptiness of consciousness, nor the practice of the signlessness of consciousness, nor the practice of the wishlessness of consciousness, nor the practice of the non-creation of consciousness;
furthermore, it is not the practice of tranquility regarding consciousness, nor is it the practice of purity regarding consciousness.
Furthermore, it is not consciousness as the practice of thorough examination;
nor is it consciousness as the practice of non-arising;
nor is it consciousness as the practice of non-origination.
Furthermore, it is not the practice of non-attachment through consciousness;
nor is it the practice of ultimate exhaustion through consciousness;
nor is it the practice of being without origin through consciousness.
This constitutes the practice of the Dharma;
yet it is not the practice of perceiving emptiness through consciousness,
nor is it the practice of perceiving the signless through consciousness.
Furthermore, it is neither the practice of consciousness nor the practice of wishlessness; this is the practice of the Dharma.
It is also not the fourfold practice;
nor is it the practice of the sense bases.
It is neither the practice of the realms of desire, form, nor formlessness; this is the dharma of practice.
It is neither practicing nor not practicing, yet it is also without practice; this is the dharma of practice.
Neither going nor not going, neither having a location nor having a place of abiding—this is the practice of the Dharma.
That which is not practiced by mind, thought, or consciousness is the practice of the Dharma.
This is what is called practicing the Dharma!
That which is practiced without seeing, hearing, or knowing is the practice of the Dharma.
If one were to be without the activities of body, speech, and mind, that is the practice of the Dharma.
To neither practice the Dharma nor practice non-Dharma is to practice the Dharma.
To have no dualistic practice and no manifold practice is to practice the Dharma.
To have no past practice, no future practice, and no present practice is to practice the Dharma.

To practice without the activity of the aggregates (*skandha*), without the activity of the elements (*dhātu*), and without the activity of the sense bases (*āyatana*)—this is the practice of the Dharma.
To practice without the activity of sensual desires, without the activity of fetters and enmity, and without the activity of discursive thoughts—this is the practice of the Dharma.

To have no practice of annihilationism and no practice of eternalism; to not attain the extremes of various views and to not rely on the Middle Way—this is the practice of the Dharma.

Whether all phenomena abide or do not abide, the locus of the self-nature of the Dharma is spontaneous; that locus, as well as its non-locus, is the locus of pure phenomena. All phenomena are unmoving, unattached, and inexhaustible; they neither exist nor are they active; they are neither frivolous nor dependent, neither non-dependent nor abiding, and they are without reception. For one who understands these phenomena with wisdom, that wisdom is free from conceptualization; this is called Truth (*satya*).

All realms that exist, Including the realm of the unconditioned;

The fundamental limit is shoreless and bottomless; one cannot reach its boundaries.

The realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha are equal;

Birth-and-death and the unconditioned—within the Way and its teachings, these are utterly tranquil.

The path of the five aggregates is likewise; there are two kinds of discerning wisdom.
Like illusory forms and images, the wise have no conceptual thoughts.
Regarding the reckoning of the four kinds, it is like the realm of empty space;
clearly understanding that nothing can be grasped, one sees the seal through the true seal.

Whatever sentient beings think, he knows it all with a single mind;

With such practice of dhāraṇī, one gathers and encompasses all phenomena.
Their fame and virtue do not conflict with their hearts, nor do they fail in their extensive learning.
Regarding all that the Buddhas of the ten directions— the Guides— have taught,

With wisdom and the various faculties, they attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Sealing all phenomena with emptiness, they are without attachment and nothing to be extracted;

The seal of space seals all phenomena, pure and devoid of anything existent;

All dharmas of causes and conditions are non-existent; causes and conditions are merely formations.

The conduct of all sentient beings, And the etiquette of forms and sounds—

the vehicle of equal and firm abiding,

The vehicle of the untainted is for the sake of selecting the category of wisdom;

the fearless vehicle is for the sake of the lion’s roar of the four fearlessnesses;

The Universal and Equal Vehicle is so called because it extends a mind of equanimous compassion toward all sentient beings;
the Harmless Vehicle is so called because it restrains all those of external paths through the True Dharma;
and the Eliminating Vehicle is so called because it subdues all the hosts of Māra.
The vehicle of quiescent extinction is for the purpose of destroying the afflictions;
the vehicle of subduing and transforming is for the purpose of overcoming the Māra of the aggregates;
the vehicle of transcendence from limits is for the purpose of surpassing the Māra of death.
The Supreme Vehicle is so called because it abandons the celestial Māras;
the Magnificent Vehicle is so called because it is able to fulfill the perfection of giving;
the Heatless Vehicle is so called because it fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline.
The vehicle that abandons enmity is so called because it is fully endowed with the perfection of patience;
the indestructible and steadfast vehicle is so called because it is fully endowed with the perfection of vigor;
the vehicle that severs all defects of self-sovereignty is so called because the mind is free from the hindrances of the aggregates.
The vehicle of cultivation is fully perfected through the perfection of tranquility;
the vehicle encountered by all virtuous qualities, all wisdom, mundane affairs, and supramundane dharmas is fully perfected through the perfection of wisdom;
and the vehicle that universally guides and accords with all vehicles is fully perfected through the perfection of skillful means.
The vehicle that reaches the ultimate reaches the ultimate because it tends toward extinction;
those who take refuge in the vehicle of peace establish the Eightfold Path;
and the vehicle that reaches the place where there is no place to go is so called because it follows and practices the contemplation of tranquility.
Those who possess the vehicle of the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment have no one—whether Māras or heterodox teachers—who can look upon them with insolence;
those who possess the vehicle of the four bases of psychic power are able to manifest universally throughout all Buddha-lands;

and those who possess the vehicle of abiding in the correct truths through equal transcendence eliminate all unwholesome dharmas and cultivate the multitude of virtuous practices and wholesome dharmas.
Those who ride the vehicle of well-cultivated and prudent mindfulness have no internal enmity;
those who ride the vehicle that does not cling even to the triple world honor the untainted (*anāsrava*);

and one who adorns the vehicle is so because their merits have been perfected.
The vehicle for those who choose according to the inclinations and natures of sentient beings is for the sake of ultimate wisdom;
the vehicle that elucidates the gateways is for the sake of not being obstructed by whatever offerings are made;
the vehicle of the single flavor is for the sake of equalizing the Buddha’s grace.
The vehicle of the great sound is so called because it is heard throughout the ten directions;
the vehicle universally honored by all devas is so called because of its excellent cultivation of practice;
the vehicle praised by Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings is so called because its virtues are immeasurable.
To those who possess stinginess and greed, one gives the vehicle of giving, for the sake of becoming a leader.

The vehicle that bestows blessings, peace, and the removal of suffering and affliction exists because it does not commit any evil;

"For this reason, it is called the Mahāyāna.

Because they are friends who do not wait to be asked by sentient beings;

speech is pure because words and actions correspond with one another.

the pure mind subdues all māras;

Because they achieve the perfection of virtue through the non-loss of supernormal powers;
because they eliminate the afflictions of sentient beings by achieving meditative concentration in profound stillness;
